questions.q: The force on a charge moving across a uniform magnetic field is always at right angles to its velocity. As the velocity direction changes, the force direction changes so that it stays perpendicular to the velocity. What motion does this produce?
options: Uniform straight-line motion, because the perpendicular force cancels out
Circular motion, because the force acts as a centripetal force, similar to the gravitational force that keeps satellites in orbit
Parabolic projectile motion, the same as a charge in a uniform electric field
The charge accelerates steadily and gains kinetic energy along the field lines
questions.explanation: Because the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, it continually redirects the charge without changing its speed, acting as a centripetal force and creating circular motion. The textbook draws the same analogy used in the episode: this is like the gravitational force that keeps satellites in orbit.

questions.q: Using F = qvB sin θ for a charge in a magnetic field, what is the force on a motionless charge sitting in the field, and on a charge that moves parallel to the field lines?
options: Both experience the maximum force F = qvB
A motionless charge (v = 0) experiences no force, and a charge moving parallel to the field lines (θ = 0, so sin θ = 0) also experiences no force
A motionless charge experiences a force but a parallel-moving charge does not
Both experience a force directed along the field lines
questions.explanation: From F = qvB sin θ, if v = 0 the force is zero, so a motionless charge in a magnetic field experiences no force. If the velocity is parallel to the field lines then θ = 0 and sin θ = 0, so that charge experiences no force either. The force is a maximum only when the velocity is perpendicular to the magnetic field lines.

questions.q: The radius of the circular path of a charged particle in a magnetic field is r = mv/Bq. How does the radius change with the particle's mass, velocity, charge and the magnetic field strength?
options: A greater mass or velocity decreases the radius; a greater charge or magnetic field strength increases it
A greater mass or velocity increases the radius, while a greater charge or magnetic field strength decreases the radius
The radius depends only on the charge and is independent of mass and velocity
A greater velocity increases the radius but mass has no effect
questions.explanation: From r = mv/Bq, the radius is proportional to mass and velocity and inversely proportional to charge and magnetic field strength. So a greater mass or velocity increases the radius, while a greater charge or magnetic field strength decreases the radius of the circular path — exactly the 'heavier or faster, bigger circle' point made in the episode.

questions.q: An electron travelling at 5.9 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ enters a uniform magnetic field of 6.0 mT, perpendicular to its velocity. What is the radius of its circular path?
questions.explanation: This is the textbook's own sample problem and the worked example from the episode: substituting into r = mv/Bq gives a radius of 5.6 mm. The magnetic field does no work, so the electron keeps the speed 5.9 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ it was given by the electron gun; the field only bends it into this small circle.

questions.q: From memory, describe how a charged particle behaves in a uniform electric field: the force on it, the direction of that force for positive and negative charges, and how its motion compares with a projectile.
keyPoints: In a uniform field a charge experiences a constant electric force F = qE, so the acceleration is also constant (F = ma).
The force on a positive charge is in the direction of the field; the force on a negative charge is opposite to the field direction.
If the charged particle is injected with speed across the field, its motion is similar to projectile motion (a parabola), like a stone falling in a gravitational field.
questions.explanation: If you recalled the constant force F = qE, the sign-dependent direction, and the analogy to projectile motion under gravity, grade yourself Good or Easy. These are the page-93 points the episode rephrases as 'electrical gravity'.

questions.q: A charged particle is initially travelling across the electric field lines between two parallel plates. According to the textbook, what is its trajectory and does the field do work on it?
options: Its trajectory is circular and the field does no work on it
Its trajectory is parabolic, similar to a projectile in a gravitational field, and as it accelerates along the field lines the field does work on the charge (W = qV), increasing its kinetic energy
Its trajectory is a straight line at constant speed because the electric force does no work
Its trajectory is parabolic but the electric field does no work because the force is perpendicular to the velocity
questions.explanation: A charge launched across the field lines keeps a constant velocity across the field while accelerating along it, giving a parabolic trajectory similar to a projectile in a gravitational field. As it accelerates along the field lines the field does work on the charge, found using W = qV (or W = qEd), increasing its kinetic energy — this is why electron guns use electric fields to accelerate electrons.

questions.q: For a satellite in a stable circular orbit, what provides the centripetal force, and what is the orbital velocity?
options: The satellite's thrust provides the centripetal force; the orbital velocity can be any value
Gravitation provides the centripetal force for orbital motion; the orbital velocity is v = √(GM/r), depending on the mass and radius of the planet
Air resistance provides the centripetal force; the orbital velocity depends only on the satellite's mass
The magnetic field provides the centripetal force; the orbital velocity is v = mv/Bq
questions.explanation: Circular motion requires a centripetal force, and gravitation provides the centripetal force for orbital motion. Equating gravity to the centripetal force gives the orbital velocity v = √(GM/r), depending on the mass and radius (and altitude) of the planet — a bigger orbit means a slower speed, as the episode notes.

questions.q: Calculate the kinetic energy of a 1500 kg satellite orbiting the Earth at a distance of 30 000 km (3.0 × 10⁷ m) from the Earth's centre. Take the mass of the Earth as 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg.
questions.explanation: This is the textbook's sample problem for orbital kinetic energy. Using E_k = GMm/2r gives 9.95 × 10⁹ J. Because gravity acts as a centripetal force perpendicular to the velocity in a circular orbit, it does no work, so this kinetic energy (and the speed) stay constant around the orbit.

questions.q: From memory: the episode reduces the whole comparison to a single question about the force. What is that question, and what does each answer determine about the path and the work done?
keyPoints: The one question: does the force stay fixed in direction, or does it stay perpendicular to the velocity?
A force fixed in direction (uniform gravity, uniform electric field) gives a parabola for a sideways-launched particle, and the field does work on it.
A force always perpendicular to the velocity (magnetic field, circular orbit) gives a circle, and the field does no work, so the speed stays constant.
questions.explanation: If you recalled the 'fixed direction vs perpendicular' distinction and linked each to its path and work outcome, grade yourself Good or Easy. The episode calls this 'the engine of the entire answer'.

questions.q: Account for the similarities and differences between the paths of masses in uniform gravitational fields, satellites in orbit, charged particles in uniform electric fields, and moving charged particles in uniform magnetic fields. (6 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: A uniform gravitational field exerts a force proportional to mass, and a uniform electric field a force proportional to charge. In both the force is constant and fixed in direction along the field and independent of velocity (though the electric force can act with or against the field depending on the sign of the charge, so it can attract or repel, whereas gravity only attracts). Because both forces are constant and fixed in direction, a particle projected across either field follows a parabola — constant velocity across the field with uniform acceleration along it — and the field does work on it, changing its kinetic energy. In contrast, the magnetic force acts only on a moving charge, depends on its speed, and is always perpendicular to the velocity; because it is perpendicular it does no work and changes only direction, producing a circle rather than a parabola. A satellite in a circular orbit bridges these: gravity here acts as a centripetal force perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work, the speed is constant, and the path is a closed circle — resembling the magnetic circle more than the gravitational parabola, even though both arise from gravity. The difference is that a projectile moves across a uniform field whereas a satellite moves through a radial, non-uniform field that continuously redirects it. Ultimately the path is set by one factor: whether the force stays fixed in direction (parabola, work done) or stays perpendicular to the velocity (circle, no work).

criteria.descriptor: Identifies that uniform gravitational and electric fields give a constant force (proportional to mass / charge), fixed in direction and independent of velocity.
States that a particle projected across either uniform field follows a parabola and that the field does work on it.
Explains the magnetic force acts only on a moving charge, depends on speed, and is always perpendicular to velocity, so it does no work and gives a circle.
Explains that a satellite in a circular orbit has gravity acting as a centripetal force perpendicular to velocity, so no work is done and the path is a circle.
Distinguishes the radial (non-uniform) orbital field from the uniform fields, using explicit comparison language (whereas / in contrast).
Reaches the unifying conclusion: fixed-direction force gives a parabola with work done, perpendicular force gives a circle with no work.

questions.explanation: The marks come from comparing by axis (force, work, path) with explicit linking words, not four separate descriptions — and from treating the radial orbit separately from the uniform-field parabolas.
